newsitem.title: ITALY: "Madmen" deride Bossi with their own joke state.
newsitem.headline: "Madmen" deride Bossi with their own joke state.

text.p: In the heart of Italy, the joke was on separatist leader Umberto Bossi as he solemnly declared independence for his would-be northern state.
A group of self-styled madmen decided to join him at his own game by proclaiming a state of their own -- for a laugh.

It was just one of many anti-secession gags staged in Italy, including one in Venice where three porn stars who had bared all in the name of unity outside Rome's parliament last week did a repeat performance on a boat in the lagoon.

In Orvieto, a central town famous for its crisp white wine, several hundred people gathered in a square to hear the "International Movement of Madmen" declare independence for "Etruria", an ancient federation of 12 Etruscan towns.
"I bet Bossi wished he could have got all these people," said the group's president, Bruno Canestri, to laughter.
Bossi staged the grand finale to his symbol-laden three-day "March to the Sea" along the River Po by declaring his would-be state of "Padania" independent at a ceremony in Venice.

In Orvieto, things were far more light-hearted. Eight men and one boy, all of whom could barely keep a straight face, stood in front of a stage rigged up in front of the town hall, wearing monk-like brown cowls, tunics and hose.

They carried ancient-looking rakes and other agricultural tools. "This is our army," Canestri said -- a dig at Bossi's green-shirted volunteer security detail and his promise on Saturday to set up a "national guard of Padania".
"But we don't want war. The Etruscans are a peaceful people," said Canestri, who runs a painting and decorating shop in the town and said he was in his 60s.

Orvieto was at the heart of the Etruscan empire in the seventh and sixth centuries BC. Little is known about the people, who had their own alphabet and became rich by mining and trading iron, copper and silver.
Shortly before the ceremony, a red aircraft flew overhead several times, dropping photocopies of the "Proclamation of the Free Etruscan Republic" in mock dialect.

Serious-looking posters around the town declared that the Secession of Etruria would include the annexation of Sardinia and other islands and would be attended by U.S. President Bill Clinton and popular Italian comic Roberto Benigni among others.
In another jibe at Bossi, who wants to take "Padania" into European monetary union without Italy, Canestri printed some fake money for his republic.

But he said his movement, which he claimed has 6,500 card- carrying members and numbers some 12,000 worldwide, had the more serious aim of raising cash to help buy equipment for Orvieto hospital and to help get young people off drugs.

While joining the laughter, Orvieto's mayor Stefano Cimicchi, who belongs to a party that is part of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition, said Bossi and his Northern League represented a serious problem.

"We had to joke about it, but we must also give a great deal of thought to the League phenomenon," he said. "The League is a phenomenon that could become dangerous...We mustn't exaggerate it, but we mustn't underestimate it either."
